items.title: 67251_Chuck Green oral history interview
items.q: Ruff Ellington's brother, I mean he -- he did East St. Louis Toodle-oo.

ctx.x: You were talking before about the different type of music that was going on at the same time. Can you tell me a little bit more about that and how it affected the tap dancers?

Yeah, well they was really trying to save the blues, you see, the blues was getting unpopular. See, because they wanted to kind of reject the blues, because the tempo of the blues, they hadn't quite came to the applying tempo, like a beat, see -- blues was more like a ballad. See? On some say it's kind of meditative. Blues. You see, until like Pop -- Ruff Ellington's brother, I mean he -- he did East St. Louis Toodle-oo. And that gave the blues a beat, you see. Someway up here in Columbus Circle there, I think he…

duce these new works by the composers from ASCAP's, you see, and the off-Broadway shows, like this thing, what was it? It was some (unintelligible) -- think they turned that out too, LEW Leslie and his partner, there. He had a partner, you see? And -- that was the darn -- name of the darned show, I think it was Zanzibar, something. It was called. And, which after those times, I mean, they was going to rename these clubs.
